patient.chief_complaint: Recurrent left arm weakness and headache — diagnosed as hemiplegic migraine; mother has MELAS
patient.hpi:
A 29-year-old Japanese woman was referred to the neurology clinic with a 2-year history of episodic left arm weakness lasting 20-40 minutes followed by a severe right-sided headache, nausea, and photophobia lasting 6-10 hours. She has had 6 episodes in 2 years. The motor symptoms spread from left hand (weakness and clumsiness) to involve the left forearm over 15-20 minutes before reaching maximum deficit. Full recovery occurs within 40-60 minutes.

The key complicating factor: her mother was diagnosed with MELAS (Mitochondrial Encephalomyopathy, Lactic Acidosis, and Stroke-like episodes) 3 years ago. The mother's MELAS was confirmed by muscle biopsy (ragged red fibres) and mitochondrial DNA analysis (m.3243A>G mutation). This has raised the concern that the daughter's episodic neurological episodes could be MELAS stroke-like episodes rather than hemiplegic migraine.

The daughter herself has mild bilateral sensorineural hearing loss (noted on audiometry at work health check). She is shorter than average (height 150cm) and her BMI is 18.8. She had mild learning difficulties at school — she struggled with mathematics. She is currently a shop assistant. She has no personal history of stroke, seizures, diabetes, or cardiac disease. She is a non-smoker, no alcohol. She has never had the m.3243A>G mutation test herself.

neurological_exam.gait: Normal gait and tandem gait. Romberg negative.
neurological_exam.additional: Audiometry documented bilateral mild sensorineural hearing loss (high-frequency pattern). No proximal muscle weakness on examination.

useless_tools.rationale: Head CT is less sensitive than MRI for migraine-relevant structural causes and is not indicated in typical migraine with aura; even when imaging is warranted, MRI is preferred
Lumbar puncture is not indicated in migraine with aura; reserve for suspected SAH (with normal CT) or meningitis — neither present here
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is not indicated in typical migraine with aura — no role unless cardioembolic stroke is on the differential

critical_actions: Test for m.3243A>G in peripheral blood and urine epithelial cells
Cardiology evaluation (echo, ECG) — mitochondrial cardiomyopathy / conduction disease screen
L-arginine for acute stroke-like episodes (off-label, low-level evidence)
contraindicated_actions: Do not prescribe triptans or ergotamines in MELAS
Do not prescribe valproate or metformin in MELAS where alternatives exist
Do not assume episodes are 'just hemiplegic migraine' in the presence of MELAS family history and red-flag features
key_reasoning_points: MELAS commonly presents with stroke-like episodes that overlap with hemiplegic migraine phenotype
Maternal inheritance pattern, short stature, sensorineural hearing loss, learning difficulty, and confirmed MELAS in mother all direct workup to m.3243A>G
MELAS-specific MRI pattern (non-vascular territory lesions, lactate peak on MRS) supports the diagnosis
Tier per the July 2026 clinical review: ICHD-3: the diagnosis is made on the structured history. Imaging is for the red flags that history screens for, not for the diagnosis.
Tier per the July 2026 clinical review: No laboratory test contributes to a migraine diagnosis; a targeted assay belongs to a specific suspicion.

July 2026 review applied end to end: ICHD-3 history/examination is required in all cases; routine MRI, EEG, ECG, CSF, echocardiography, cardiac monitoring and laboratory panels are absent. Retained tests answer an explicit atypical-aura, seizure, infarct, MELAS, CADASIL or aneurysm question.

red_herrings.data_point: Episodic left arm weakness with gradual onset and subsequent headache — hemiplegic migraine pattern
red_herrings.intended_effect: Gradual motor arm weakness over 15-20 minutes followed by severe headache is a classic hemiplegic migraine description
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: MELAS stroke-like episodes can present identically; MELAS clues (maternal inheritance of MELAS, bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, short stature, elevated lactate) distinguish MELAS from hemiplegic migraine; m.3243A>G confirmed

red_herrings.data_point: Mother has MELAS — patient may have hemiplegic migraine (different condition from MELAS)
red_herrings.intended_effect: MELAS and hemiplegic migraine are different disorders; having a parent with MELAS does not mean the patient has MELAS (though maternal transmission is the mechanism)
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: m.3243A>G is maternally transmitted — the patient inherited it from her mother; mutation confirmed in patient's own testing; MELAS diagnosis established

interactions: Triptans are 5-HT1B/1D agonists causing vasoconstriction — in MELAS, stroke-like episodes result from energy failure in cerebrovascular endothelium; vasoconstriction may worsen ischaemia during episodes
contraindications: Triptans CONTRAINDICATED in MELAS — vasoconstrictive mechanism worsens stroke-like episode severity and duration
warnings: Metformin is generally contraindicated in mitochondrial disorders due to risk of lactic acidosis exacerbation
